refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: systemd-keyring-setup.service is an early boot service that enrolls X.509 certificates into the kernel keyrings used to verify signatures on dm-verity volumes, fs-verity files and BPF programs, and then seals these keyrings. The certificates are read from the File Hierarchy for the Verification of OS Artifacts (VOA). This allows the kernel to verify signatures with keys provided by the OS vendor or the local administrator, without rebuilding the kernel and without enrolling the keys into the firmware.
The following keyrings are provisioned, each from a VOA context of the kernel-keyring purpose:

row.entry: Signatures of the root hashes of dm-verity volumes, such as those of Discoverable Disk Images set up by systemd-veritysetup@.service8, systemd-dissect1 or the RootImage= setting of services
Built-in signatures of fs-verity protected files

refsect1.para: The kernel only uses the .dm-verity and .bpf keyrings once they have been sealed, and seals them itself while they are still empty, unless dm_verity.keyring_unsealed=1 or bpf.keyring_unsealed=1 is specified on the kernel command line, respectively. Hence, these options are required to provision the two keyrings, see below. The .fs-verity keyring is not sealed by the kernel, and is used as soon as it contains a key.

For each keyring that is not sealed yet, the service enrolls the certificates it finds and then seals the keyring: it installs a restriction so that only certificates signed by a key in the keyring can be added afterwards, and removes the permission to change this restriction or the permissions of the keyring. The keyring is sealed even if no certificates were found, or if some of them could not be enrolled. Keys that were already in the keyring before the service ran are sealed in as well, and a warning is logged about them.

The service runs both in the initrd and on the host. Usually, the keyrings are provisioned in the initrd, since the root file system might itself be a dm-verity volume that is verified with one of the enrolled keys. When the service runs again on the host, the keyrings have been sealed already. In this case, only certificates signed by a key that was enrolled earlier can be added, and all other certificates are rejected. Certificates that have been enrolled already are skipped.

refsect1.title: Certificate Directories and Precedence
refsect1.para: Certificates are read from the VOA load paths /etc/voa/, /run/voa/, /usr/local/share/voa/ and /usr/share/voa/, in order of decreasing priority. For each keyring, artifact verifiers are read from OS/kernel-keyring/CONTEXT/x509/NAME-certificate.pem, and trust anchors from OS/trust-anchor-kernel-keyring/CONTEXT/x509/NAME-certificate.pem below each load path. Both are enrolled into the same keyring. NAME may consist of lowercase letters, digits, ., _ and -, other files are ignored. Each file must contain a single PEM-encoded certificate. A file that contains more than one certificate is ignored as a whole. CA certificates should be placed in separate files among the trust anchors instead.

Certificates are looked up for two OS identifiers derived from os-release5: the exact identifier, and the value of ID= alone. The exact identifier consists of the values of ID=, VERSION_ID=, VARIANT_ID=, IMAGE_ID= and IMAGE_VERSION=, separated by :. A field that is not set is left empty, and unset fields at the end are omitted. For example, ID=debian and VERSION_ID=13 result in the identifiers debian:13 and debian. If ID= is not set, linux is used. If one of the other fields contains characters that are not permitted by the VOA specification, only the value of ID= is used. If ID= itself contains such characters, no certificates are looked up.

Note that the VOA specification requires different semantics than the usual logic for configuration files, where a file in a directory with higher priority replaces a file with the same name in a directory with lower priority. Instead, X.509 certificates are merged: all files in all load paths are used. A certificate that is found in more than one place is only enrolled once. If two different certificates have the same subject and key identifier, only one of them can be added to a keyring. In this case, certificates found for the exact OS identifier take precedence over the ones found for the value of ID= alone, and among those, the certificate from the load path with the highest priority is enrolled.

A certificate may be masked by placing a symlink to /dev/null with the same file name in any of the load paths, usually in /etc/voa/ or /run/voa/. As required by the VOA specification, a masked certificate is ignored in all load paths, including the ones with a higher priority than the one containing the symlink. Masking is meant as a substitute for revocation: if a certificate is considered compromised, a single symlink ensures that none of its copies is enrolled. Other symlinks are followed as long as they point to a location within the VOA hierarchy, and symlinks to certificate files only if the target has the same file name.

To make sure that certificates cannot be placed by unprivileged users, files that are executable or writable by anyone but their owner, and directories that are writable by anyone but their owner, are ignored. Once a directory owned by an unprivileged user has been entered, the lookup does not continue into files or directories owned by anyone else.

refsect1.title: Options
refsect1.para: If one or more KEYRING names, such as .dm-verity, are specified, only those keyrings are processed. Otherwise, all keyrings listed above are processed.

listitem.para: Show which certificates would be enrolled into which keyring, and the current state of the keyrings, without changing anything.

refsect1.title: Exit status
refsect1.para: On success, 0 is returned. This includes the cases where a keyring does not exist, or has been provisioned by an earlier run already. If a certificate could not be used, for example because it is malformed, or because it is not signed by a key in a keyring that has been sealed already, 65 (EX_DATAERR) is returned. systemd-keyring-setup.service treats this exit status as success. On other failures, a different non-zero exit status is returned.

listitem.para: These options are interpreted by the kernel. If set to 1, the kernel leaves the .dm-verity or .bpf keyring unsealed during boot, so that it can be provisioned by systemd-keyring-setup.service. Otherwise, the kernel seals the keyring while it is still empty, and no certificates can be enrolled into it.

refsect1.title: Security Considerations
refsect1.para: The enrolled certificates can only be trusted as much as the files they were read from. The intended deployment is to provision the keyrings from the initrd of a signed Unified Kernel Image, see systemd-stub7.

Until a keyring is sealed, any sufficiently privileged process may add arbitrary keys to it. After it has been sealed, privileged processes may still remove keys from it, and add certificates that are signed by a key in the keyring, but they cannot add other keys, or change the restriction or the permissions of the keyring. The keyrings stay sealed until the next reboot. A soft reboot, see systemd-soft-reboot.service8, does not reset them.

If dm-verity is built as a kernel module, unloading and reloading the module discards the .dm-verity keyring, including its seal, and creates a new, empty one. If dm_verity.keyring_unsealed=1 is set, the new keyring may then be provisioned with arbitrary keys again. systemd-keyring-setup logs a warning if a keyring belongs to a loadable kernel module. For high-security setups, dm-verity should be built into the kernel.
